summary: We have partially created a partially story mode game. Our idea was to make an interactive and fun game that allows players to both learn concepts and use their knowledge of building space missions from picking the goal all the way to analysing the data through an emotionally engaging story of the protagonist who continues to cement his dad's legacy by working on his dad's abandoned projects. The game uses lego-like blocks and models allowing the user to build rockets, satellites and rovers with familiarity. The game runs a simplified simulation engine that lets the user experiment with different parameters and see effects on the mission that are life-like. The game is set in the 70s in an era where humans have not yet explored the moon. The protagonist must first work on other projects to gain skills and climb the career-ladder to gain enough influence in the space organisation to reboot his father's abandoned project. We planned to show this by having 3 levels. The game directly allows users to understand rocket-design, rover design, satellite design and all aspects of space mission design throughout the 3 levels to young gamers aspiring to be engineers and scientists in the future. Currently however over the course of 2 days we have only been able to get the game engine running, a low-poly map and a script for the storyline.
details:
PROJECT DAEDALUS is a story-driven LEGO space game where you explore a space organisation's facility, build and test a rocket, then launch it to complete missions. The player designs a rocket from parts; the simulation uses stored engineering data and calculation scripts to estimate thrust, stability, cost, and whether the rocket can reach orbit. In the story, those results affect mission progress and the launch outcome. We used both a theoretical simulation and real life data from past NASA space missions to calculate a score of how good (broadly speaking) a player's rocket will be, determining whether the mission will fail or succeed.

The game also has an engaging emotional arc with relations to the protagonist's father, the previous mission lead for the project. Players progress from team lead engineer—designing a satellite to photograph the Moon—to principal engineer, leading a department and planning a monkey’s lunar mission, then chief program technologist, guiding the engineering strategy for a human Moon mission. Each level turns real engineering ideas into approachable design choices, with the simulation calculating performance and mission success behind the scenes.

We deliberately chose a LEGO-style theme for this game. Our audience is young learners, aspiring engineers, and future astronauts, and for them, building with interlocking blocks is already a familiar and intuitive activity. Because they don’t have to learn a complicated new interface, they can put their attention on what matters: the real challenges of space mission design.

The block-based format also gives players room to be creative. They can design their own rockets, test different configurations, and see for themselves how their choices affect the outcome. Learning happens through experimentation rather than instruction, so mistakes become part of the process instead of setbacks.

Beyond rocket design, the game introduces other parts of a space mission, such as planning, resource management, and strategic decision-making. Players come to see that a successful mission depends on both sound engineering and careful strategy.

Our aim is to encourage young gamers and learners to experience both sides of space mission design in an environment that feels approachable, engaging, and fun, and to inspire the next generation of engineers and explorers.We have used chatgpt's codex and claude-code for paritally coding and debugging the game, made using godot's game engine and GDscript. We have also used brick-link's studio to design lego models for the game as well as using open source models available online.

Our project combines simplified rocket and satellite design with a personal story about a child, an absent father, and a space program trying to recover from a past failure. The team considered scientific accuracy, approachable gameplay, period-inspired LEGO visuals, and the emotional weight of balancing family, ambition, and responsibility
